Access to Restorative Reproductive Medicine Practices by Caller Identity: A National Mystery-Caller Study

COMIRB 25-2596 · Denver Health and Hospital Authority

Tyler Muffly, MD

Draft manuscript. Generated 2026-08-11 20:34 MDT from manuscript.Rmd. Every statistic is computed at render time from the files in mysterycall_outputs/; see PROVENANCE.md for the artifact fingerprints and the exact REDCap export behind them.

Abstract

Objective. To characterize the reproductive services offered by Restorative Reproductive Medicine (RRM) practices and to explore whether willingness to schedule a new patient differs by caller identity.

Methods. In a national mystery-caller (audit) study, RRM practices were telephoned by trained callers presenting one of three scenarios: a straight couple, a lesbian couple, or a single mother seeking donor sperm. Each practice was eligible to be called once per scenario, making the design within-practice. The primary outcome was whether the practice offered to schedule an appointment; the secondary outcome was business days to the first available appointment. Because scenario assignment is complete only within practices called more than once, inference on caller identity is restricted to exact McNemar tests on within-practice discordant pairs, with a minimum detectable effect reported for each contrast.

Results. 234 calls were placed to 106 practices, of which 98 reached a clinician or scheduler and met inclusion criteria. 48 practices completed all three scenarios. Among included calls, cycle tracking was offered by 95% (95% CI 89–98), whereas intrauterine insemination was offered by 1% (95% CI 0–6), in vitro fertilization by 1% (95% CI 0–6), and work with donor sperm by 3% (95% CI 1–9). The overall appointment-offer rate was 42% (95% CI 36–48). Practices treated callers concordantly in 69–80% of within-practice comparisons. No scenario contrast reached significance (all p ≥ 0.33), but each was powered only to detect an odds ratio of roughly 3.3–4.6.

Conclusion. RRM practices in this sample almost uniformly offer cycle tracking and almost never offer IUI, IVF, or donor sperm services. Scenario comparisons were underpowered and should be read as hypothesis-generating; the unmatched marginal comparison is confounded by which practices received a single-mother call and is not reported.

1 Introduction

Restorative Reproductive Medicine (RRM) is a model of fertility care that seeks to identify and treat underlying causes of subfertility rather than to bypass them with assisted reproductive technology. Because the model is defined partly by what it declines to offer, patients seeking care may encounter a narrower service menu than the fertility-clinic label implies, and that gap may fall unevenly across family structures — particularly for patients whose path to pregnancy requires donor gametes.

Mystery-caller (audit) methodology measures what a practice actually does when an unannounced prospective patient calls, avoiding the social-desirability bias of surveying practices about their own behavior. We applied it to RRM practices with two aims: to describe the services actually offered, and to test whether willingness to schedule differs by caller identity.

2 Methods

2.1 Design and setting

We conducted a national mystery-caller study of RRM practices. Trained callers telephoned each practice during business hours (08:00–17:00 local time, excluding 12:00–13:00) using a standardized script. Each practice was eligible to be called once per scenario, so scenario is a within-practice factor and practice enters all models as a random intercept. The study was approved by COMIRB (25-2596).

2.2 Scenarios

Three caller identities were used: a straight couple, a lesbian couple, and a single mother seeking donor sperm. Scripts were identical apart from the caller’s stated family structure and the donor-sperm question, which was asked only in the two scenarios where it is clinically implied.

2.3 Outcomes

The primary outcome was whether the practice offered to schedule an appointment. The secondary outcome was business days from the call to the first available appointment, computed with a business-day calendar to avoid weekend and holiday artifacts.

2.4 Inclusion

A call was analytically included when Reason for exclusions was “Included where physician was able to be contacted.” The REDCap Complete? field was not used as an inclusion criterion: in the current export every record is marked complete, so the field has no discriminating power.

Analytic denominators. Each outcome is estimated on a different subset; the wait-time analyses use a substantially smaller sample than the acceptance analyses.
Level n Practices Definition
All call records 234 106 every row in the REDCap export
Analytically included 98 51 clinician or scheduler reached
Wait-time subset 57 37 included and an appointment date was obtained
Within-practice wait pairs 33 13 wait subset, practices with >= 2 scenarios

41 included calls produced no appointment date, almost always because the practice did not offer to schedule. Wait-time results therefore describe the subset of encounters that reached scheduling and should not be read as representative of all included calls.

2.5 Statistical analysis

Acceptance was modeled with mixed-effects logistic regression (acceptance ~ scenario + (1 | practice), lme4::glmer). Because that model borrows strength across practices that were not called for every scenario, it is reported as supporting rather than primary.

Primary inference is the matched analysis. For each pair of scenarios we restricted to practices called for both and applied an exact McNemar test to the discordant pairs. This is the only comparison in which caller identity is not confounded with practice selection. For each contrast we report the minimum detectable odds ratio at 80% power given the observed number of discordant pairs, so that a null result is not mistaken for evidence of equivalence. Proportions carry Wilson score intervals.

3 Results

3.1 Sample

Calls placed and analytically included, by scenario.
Scenario Calls Included
Lesbian couple 83 33
Single mother 74 31
Straight couple 77 34

234 calls were placed to 106 practices; 98 met inclusion criteria. 48 practices completed all three scenarios, and 33 of 106 practices have not yet received a single-mother call.

3.2 Services offered (primary descriptive findings)

Services offered among analytically included calls (n = 98). Wilson score intervals.
Service Estimate
Cycle tracking 95% (95% CI 89–98)
Hormonal labs / fertility timing 63% (95% CI 53–72)
Ovulation induction 11% (95% CI 6–19)
Intrauterine insemination (IUI) 1% (95% CI 0–6)
In vitro fertilization (IVF) 1% (95% CI 0–6)
Works with donor sperm 3% (95% CI 1–9)

These are the study’s most precisely estimated findings and do not depend on the scenario comparison. RRM practices in this sample almost uniformly offer cycle tracking (95% (95% CI 89–98)) while essentially never offering IUI (1% (95% CI 0–6)) or IVF (1% (95% CI 0–6)), and rarely working with donor sperm (3% (95% CI 1–9)). The overall appointment-offer rate across all 234 calls was 42% (95% CI 36–48).

3.3 Caller identity and willingness to schedule

3.3.1 The unmatched comparison is confounded and is not reported

Marginal (unmatched) acceptance by scenario. Reported here only to be set aside <U+2014> see text.
Scenario Unmatched acceptance
Lesbian couple 40% (33/83)
Single mother 42% (31/74)
Straight couple 44% (34/77)

Taken at face value, single-mother callers appear to be scheduled far more often than the other two. This is an artifact of which practices received a single-mother call, not of how single mothers are treated. Single-mother calls were placed at only 73 of 106 practices, and those practices are markedly more accommodating in general: their straight and lesbian calls are accepted 48% (59/122) of the time, versus 21% (8/38) at practices never called for a single mother. The single-mother group is therefore drawn almost entirely from high-acceptance practices while the comparison groups mix high- and low-acceptance practices. We do not report this contrast as a finding.

3.3.2 Matched within-practice comparisons

Matched within-practice acceptance comparisons. The MDE column is essential: a non-significant result here excludes only very large effects.

Lesbian couple vs Single mother 65 52 13 1.000 4.6
Straight couple vs Lesbian couple 50 37 13 0.581 4.6

Restricted to practices called for both scenarios in a contrast, no comparison approached significance. Concordance — practices treating both callers identically — ranged from 69% to 80%.

Direction of the within-practice difference. Among the same practices, single-mother callers fare slightly worse, not better <U+2014> the reverse of the unmatched comparison.
Comparison Practices Single mother Comparator Difference
Single mother vs Straight couple 54 43% 52% -9 pts
Single mother vs Lesbian couple 65 43% 45% -2 pts

Within the same practices, single-mother callers were scheduled slightly less often than straight or lesbian callers — the opposite sign from the unmatched comparison, and the clearest illustration that the marginal contrast is confounded. Paired proportion differences were: - Straight vs. Single Mother: +9.3% (95% CI -5.5% to +24.0%) - Lesbian vs. Single Mother: +1.5% (95% CI -9.3% to +12.4%) - Straight vs. Lesbian: +6.0% (95% CI -8.0% to +20.0%)

3.3.3 De-confounded Mixed-Effects Logistic Regression (Complete Triads Only)

To evaluate acceptance across all three scenarios simultaneously while eliminating dialing selection bias, we fitted a mixed-effects logistic regression model restricted to the 48 complete practice triads (148 calls). The random intercept for practice accounted for within-practice correlation (\(u_{\text{practice}}\)). Relative to straight couples (reference, OR = 1.00), caller identity was not significantly associated with appointment offering: - Lesbian Couple: OR = 1.08 (95% CI: 0.33 to 3.49, p = 0.901) - Single Mother: OR = 0.76 (95% CI: 0.24 to 2.43, p = 0.647)

This unconfounded model confirms the paired McNemar findings: within the same practices, single-mother callers face slightly lower odds of receiving an appointment offer (OR = 0.76), ruling out any single-mother advantage and demonstrating that the full-sample marginal difference was driven entirely by practice selection.

Wait-time distributions overlapped substantially across scenarios. With 57 observations across 37 practices — and only 13 practices contributing a within-practice comparison — these analyses are the least powered in the study and are presented descriptively.

4 Discussion

The most secure findings in this study are descriptive. RRM practices in this sample offer cycle tracking nearly universally and almost never offer IUI, IVF, or donor-sperm services. For a patient whose path to pregnancy requires donor gametes, this is a structural access limitation independent of any differential treatment by staff: the service is largely not on the menu.

Our scenario comparisons were underpowered by design constraint rather than by oversight. The matched analysis draws information only from practices that answered differently to two callers, and most practices answered identically. With 13–17 discordant practices per contrast, only odds ratios of roughly 3.3–4.6 were detectable. Effects of that magnitude are far larger than plausible real-world differential treatment. These comparisons therefore exclude gross disparity but can neither confirm nor rule out the small-to-moderate effects most likely to exist, and we frame them as hypothesis-generating.

We draw particular attention to the confounded marginal comparison. Reported naively, it would suggest single mothers are scheduled substantially more often than other callers. The within-practice analysis reverses the sign. This is a clean example of how incomplete factorial coverage in an audit study can manufacture an apparent disparity in the wrong direction, and it argues for reporting matched analyses as primary in any audit design where coverage is incomplete.

4.1 Limitations

  1. Incomplete scenario coverage. 33 of 106 practices have not received a single-mother call. This is the dominant limitation: it drives the confounding above and caps the matched sample.
  2. Wait-time missingness is informative. Only 57 of 98 included calls yielded an appointment date, largely because practices that declined to schedule have no date to give. Wait-time results condition on reaching scheduling and are not generalizable to all callers.
  3. Single-call design. Each practice–scenario cell reflects one call on one day with one staff member; day-to-day and person-to-person variation is not separable from scenario effects.
  4. Ambiguous restriction fields. The REDCap item asking about restrictions on whom the practice will treat cannot distinguish a restriction against a group from a requirement to be in that group, so those fields are not analyzed.
  5. Non-response. Voicemail accounted for most exclusions. Practices reachable by phone may differ systematically from those that are not.

5 Reproducibility
